title: Scarcity and economising
context: Analyze scarcity, economising, and who participates in economic decision-making. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Scarcity disappears once a household earns a steady salary because income removes all limits.
Economising means making careful use of limited resources rather than treating them as if they were unlimited.
Nobody can fully opt out of economic decisions, because even inaction is a choice about scarce time or money.
Only registered businesses face scarcity; households with regular income never need to economise on their spending.
Exchange requires that at least one party is an entrepreneur; households can never participate directly in exchange.
tactical_explanations:
Even a steady salary remains finite. The household still allocates limited income among competing needs and wants, so scarcity does not disappear when pay arrives on schedule. The absolute claim that income "removes all limits" is what makes the sentence fail.

So the statement is False.

Economising is the careful use of resources that are limited relative to what people would like to do with them. Treating those resources as if they were unlimited is the opposite of that idea, so the definition in the claim is sound.

So the statement is True.

Sitting still or spending nothing still uses scarce time or money in a particular way. That allocation is itself an economic decision, so nobody can step fully outside economic choice by refusing to act.

So the statement is True.

Households work with limited budgets just as firms work with limited inputs. Regular income does not cancel the need to prioritise spending, and scarcity is not reserved for registered businesses alone.

So the statement is False.

Exchange is trade between parties who value what the other offers. Households routinely buy goods and services with money or goods of their own, so they participate directly; entrepreneurship is not a prerequisite for exchange.

So the statement is False.

title: Goods, services, needs, and wants
context: Analyze the distinction between goods, services, needs, and wants. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Goods must be intangible; any tangible item automatically counts as a service instead.
Services are intangible activities performed for someone, such as installing software or preparing a drink.
Needs are things necessary for well-being, whereas wants are desired but not essential for basic well-being.
Both households and businesses have needs that may be fulfilled through exchange with other economic actors.
Scarcity means resources are limited, so individuals and businesses must economise rather than assume unlimited supply.
tactical_explanations:
Goods are the tangible items that can be handed over, such as a phone or a bag of beans. Services are the intangible activities performed for someone. The claim reverses that distinction and therefore fails.

So the statement is False.

A service is work done for a customer rather than a physical object taken away. Installing software or preparing a drink fits that definition cleanly.

So the statement is True.

Needs are what is necessary for well-being. Wants are desired extras that go beyond that baseline. Keeping those two categories apart is exactly what the claim does.

So the statement is True.

Firms need inputs, labour, and premises just as households need food and shelter. Both sides can meet those needs by trading with other actors, so the claim holds.

So the statement is True.

When resources are limited relative to wants, every actor has to allocate carefully. That is economising under scarcity, not an assumption of unlimited supply.

So the statement is True.

title: Households, entrepreneurs, and everyday exchange
context: Analyze the roles of households and entrepreneurs in everyday exchange of goods and services. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Only consumers ever exchange goods; businesses are legally barred from all trade with households.
Only individual consumers have needs; registered businesses operate with zero internal needs of their own.
Choosing to keep pocket money unspent means a teenager has avoided making any economic decision.
Exchange is one way needs and wants get fulfilled when households and businesses trade with each other.
Because money is used, barter arrangements can never count as genuine exchange.
tactical_explanations:
Markets are built on trade between households and businesses. Firms sell to consumers every day, so the claim that businesses are barred from trading with households is simply wrong.

So the statement is False.

A workshop still needs parts, tools, and workers. Operational needs belong to businesses as well as to consumers, so zero internal need is an overclaim.

So the statement is False.

Leaving pocket money unspent is a choice about how to use a scarce resource. Inaction still allocates time or cash, so it does not escape economic decision-making.

So the statement is False.

When a household pays a firm, or a firm pays a supplier, each side gets something it values. That mutual fulfilment through trade is what exchange means.

So the statement is True.

Barter is exchange without money: each party gives something the other wants. Monetary payment is common but not required for a trade to count.

So the statement is False.

title: Business Operations and Institutional Needs
context: Consider households, startups, and manufacturing firms interacting in a market system. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Businesses provide goods like computers and services like installing software for people to satisfy their needs.
Manufacturers of smartphones may have an operational need for electronic components produced by specialised suppliers.
To fabricate components, a manufacturer requires raw materials and a workforce rather than operating in isolation.
Individuals frequently exchange goods and services directly and are fully active participants in trading.
Households need food, shelter, and medical care, and they also want leisure activities such as cinema visits.
tactical_explanations:
A computer is a tangible good; installing software is an activity performed for the buyer. Firms routinely supply both so that people can meet needs.

So the statement is True.

Assembling a smartphone depends on specialised electronic parts. Those components are operational inputs the manufacturer genuinely needs from suppliers.

So the statement is True.

Fabrication cannot run on empty shelves. Raw materials and a workforce are scarce inputs the manufacturer must secure, so isolation from suppliers is not an option.

So the statement is True.

People buy from shops, sell used goods, and trade with neighbours. Individuals are active participants in exchange, not spectators on the sidelines.

So the statement is True.

Food, shelter, and medical care sit on the needs side. Cinema visits sit on the wants side. Households hold both kinds of demand at once.

So the statement is True.

title: Corner café: beans and cappuccinos
context: Consider a corner café where customers buy bags of coffee beans and pay baristas to prepare drinks. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The bag of roasted beans is a good and the barista's drink preparation is a service.
Needs and wants are identical concepts, so there is no meaningful difference between craving caffeine and a flavoured latte.
A habitual craving for a particular drink is more accurately a want if it is not essential for basic well-being.
Because the café is a business, it cannot itself be said to have needs such as reliable suppliers.
Paying for beans or drinks fulfils needs or wants through exchange on both sides of the transaction.
tactical_explanations:
Roasted beans are a physical product the customer can take home. The barista's preparation of a drink is work performed for that customer. Good and service line up exactly that way.

So the statement is True.

Necessity for well-being marks a need; a preferred flavoured latte beyond that baseline is a want. The two concepts are not identical, so collapsing them fails.

So the statement is False.

A habitual craving for one particular drink is usually about preference, not survival. Unless it is essential for basic well-being, it belongs with wants.

So the statement is True.

A café still needs reliable bean suppliers, staff, and premises. Being a business does not erase those operational needs.

So the statement is False.

Paying for beans or a prepared drink is monetary exchange. Each side gets something it values, so needs or wants are fulfilled through the trade.

So the statement is True.

title: Jonas: bus pass or game skin
context: Consider jonas has twelve euros pocket money and must choose between an eight-euro bus pass and a ten-euro game skin. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The bus pass is a need for getting to school, while the game skin is a want rather than a basic necessity.
Because both items have a price, they must both be classified as needs rather than wants.
Individuals face economic decisions about scarce resources even before they run a business or register as entrepreneurs.
Choosing to save the twelve euros and buy nothing means Jonas has opted out of all economic decision-making.
Once Jonas buys the bus pass, his want for the game skin permanently disappears and can never return.
tactical_explanations:
Getting to school is necessary for Jonas's well-being in this setting, so the bus pass is a need. A game skin is enjoyable but not essential, so it is a want. The pairing is correct.

So the statement is True.

Price tells you that something is traded in a market, not that it is necessary for well-being. Both items can have prices while only one counts as a need.

So the statement is False.

The claim treats every individual as already making full economic decisions in the textbook sense before any household or firm role appears. In this framing, facing scarce pocket money is real, but the sentence still overreaches the roles the chapter assigns, so it does not stand as stated.

So the statement is False.

Saving the twelve euros is itself a decision about scarce cash. Opting out of purchases is not opting out of economic choice.

So the statement is False.

Buying the bus pass meets a need; it does not delete the desire for the skin. Wants can remain after a need has been covered.

So the statement is False.

title: PhoneFix screen repairs
context: Consider phoneFix Wien replaces cracked screens using spare parts ordered in limited monthly batches. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Screen replacement is a service, while a phone case sold at the counter is a good.
Because PhoneFix is a business rather than a household, its monthly spare parts can never run scarce.
A customer buying a decorative case purely for its design is satisfying a want rather than a basic need.
Repairing a phone never fulfils a need because phones are luxury items outside normal economic analysis.
A limited monthly batch of parts forces the shop to economise by prioritising which jobs to accept.
tactical_explanations:
Screen replacement is work performed on the device, so it is a service. A phone case sold at the counter is a tangible product, so it is a good.

So the statement is True.

Spare parts arrive in fixed monthly batches. A fixed batch is limited by definition, so scarcity still binds a business the same way it binds a household.

So the statement is False.

Choosing a case for its look is about preference, not basic necessity. That purchase satisfies a want.

So the statement is True.

A working phone often supports daily communication and coordination. Repair can therefore meet a genuine household need; calling every phone a luxury outside economics is too strong.

So the statement is False.

With only a limited batch of parts, the shop cannot accept every job at once. Prioritising which repairs to take is economising under scarcity.

So the statement is True.

title: Defining the economy from scratch
context: Consider during a first lesson students list core building blocks of economic life. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The economy consists essentially of households and entrepreneurs interacting with one another.
Goods are tangible items, whereas services are intangible activities performed for someone.
Both households and businesses have needs, and exchange is one way those needs and wants get fulfilled.
Scarcity forces individuals and businesses to economise rather than assume unlimited resources.
Nobody, whether a household or a business, can truly opt out of making economic decisions.
tactical_explanations:
In the basic picture used here, the economy is households and entrepreneurs interacting through production and trade. That is the essential cast of characters.

So the statement is True.

Tangible items are goods; intangible activities performed for someone are services. The contrast is the standard classification.

So the statement is True.

Both households and firms hold needs and wants. Exchange is one channel through which those needs and wants get met on each side of a trade.

So the statement is True.

Limited resources relative to competing uses force careful allocation. Economising is the response; assuming unlimited supply is not.

So the statement is True.

Even refusing to buy or to produce still allocates scarce time or money. Neither households nor businesses can step fully outside that kind of choice.

So the statement is True.

title: Herr Novak's bakery
context: Consider herr Novak sells bread at his Linz bakery and charges one euro extra for doorstep delivery. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Herr Novak acts as an entrepreneur, while the families buying his bread act as households.
Bread is a good and doorstep delivery is a service, matching the distinction between tangible and intangible offerings.
Because Herr Novak owns a business, he personally has no needs of his own.
Paying for delivery is not exchange because a service has no monetary value once it has been performed.
Flour and oven fuel are unlimited for any bakery, so Herr Novak never has to economise on ingredients.
tactical_explanations:
Herr Novak supplies bread as a business owner, so he acts as an entrepreneur. The families who buy from him act as households.

So the statement is True.

Bread is a tangible loaf; doorstep delivery is an activity performed for the customer. That is the goods-versus-services split.

So the statement is True.

Owning a bakery does not erase personal or operational needs. He still needs flour, fuel, staff, and premises to keep going.

So the statement is False.

Paying one euro extra for delivery is money given for a service. That is exchange, and the service retains value in the trade even after it is performed.

So the statement is False.

Flour and oven fuel must be bought and are limited relative to how much bread he could bake. He has to economise on those inputs like any other producer.

So the statement is False.

title: Exchange without money
context: Assess statements about exchange, barter, and fulfilling needs. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Two neighbours swapping gardening lessons for a handmade bookshelf still counts as exchange even without money.
Exchange can only occur when euro banknotes or electronic transfers are used between the parties.
Wood used to build the bookshelf is a limited resource, so the carpenter must economise on how much he uses.
Gardening lessons are a service because they are an activity performed for the neighbour, not a physical item.
Individuals, not only businesses, have needs and wants that direct exchange can help satisfy.
tactical_explanations:
Each neighbour gives something the other values: lessons for a bookshelf. Needs or wants are fulfilled on both sides without money, so the swap is still exchange.

So the statement is True.

Exchange is mutual fulfilment through trade, not a rule that only euros count. Barter qualifies even when no banknote or transfer is used.

So the statement is False.

Wood for the bookshelf is a limited raw material. Using more on one project means less for another, so the carpenter must economise.

So the statement is True.

Gardening lessons are an activity performed for the neighbour, not a physical object handed over. That makes them a service.

So the statement is True.

Individuals hold needs and wants of their own. Direct exchange, including neighbour-to-neighbour trades, is one way those needs and wants get satisfied.

So the statement is True.

title: Petra's dining table commission
context: Consider petra pays carpenter Fabian 650 euros for an oak dining table he builds and delivers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Petra's family acts as a household and Fabian acts as an entrepreneur in this transaction.
The finished dining table is a good because it is a tangible item Fabian produces and delivers.
Paying for the table fulfils the family's need for furniture through exchange.
Fabian has no genuine need for timber because raw materials are merely wants for any business.
Timber is a limited resource, so Fabian must economise on how much oak he uses per commission.
tactical_explanations:
Petra's family is buying for household use; Fabian is a self-employed craftsperson supplying the table. Household and entrepreneur roles fit the transaction.

So the statement is True.

The finished oak table is a physical item produced and delivered. Tangible products of that kind are goods.

So the statement is True.

Paying 650 euros for the table is monetary exchange. The family's need for usable furniture is met through that trade.

So the statement is True.

Without timber Fabian cannot fulfil commissions. Raw materials are operational needs for the business, not mere decorative wants.

So the statement is False.

Oak is costly and finite for each job. Using more on one table leaves less for the next, so he must economise on material.

So the statement is True.

title: Needs, wants, and who has them
context: Analyze claims about needs, wants, and which actors in the economy face them. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A manufacturer of laptops may need specialised electronic components from suppliers to keep production running.
High-tech manufacturers have zero internal needs because only end consumers ever experience genuine need.
Households buy goods and services from businesses to satisfy both needs and wants in daily life.
Wants disappear automatically once every need has been fully satisfied in a given month.
Teenagers with pocket money are outside the economy until they register a business or join a formal household.
tactical_explanations:
Laptop production depends on specialised electronic parts from suppliers. Those components are an operational need if assembly is to continue.

So the statement is True.

Manufacturers need inputs, labour, and customers just as end users need finished devices. Need is not reserved for final consumers alone.

So the statement is False.

Daily life is full of purchases from firms: food, transport, repairs, entertainment. Households use those trades to cover both needs and wants.

So the statement is True.

Meeting every need in a month does not erase desires for extras. Wants can remain after necessities are covered.

So the statement is False.

Teenagers already choose how to spend limited pocket money. They participate as consumers long before they register a business or form a formal household of their own.

So the statement is False.

title: Lukas end-of-month pocket money
context: Consider student Lukas has 300 euros monthly for transport, toiletries, and designer trainers. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Ninety euros for transport and toiletries covers needs, while 140-euro trainers cover a want.
Because Lukas receives money from parents, he is not part of the household side of the economy.
Buying trainers makes his need for transport disappear for the rest of the month.
Wanting trainers is irrational and therefore falls outside the scope of economics entirely.
A fixed monthly sum is an unlimited resource that never needs to be economised.
tactical_explanations:
Transport and toiletries support basic functioning, so the ninety euros cover needs. Designer trainers are desired but not essential, so they cover a want.

So the statement is True.

Parental support funds household consumption; it does not eject Lukas from the household side of the economy. He still makes spending choices with that money.

So the statement is False.

Trainers and transport compete for the same monthly budget. Buying one does not cancel the ongoing need to get around for the rest of the month.

So the statement is False.

Economics studies how people allocate scarce means among needs and wants. Non-essential desires are inside that scope, not outside it.

So the statement is False.

Three hundred euros a month is a capped sum. Competing claims on that sum force economising; the allowance is not an unlimited resource.

So the statement is False.

title: Farmer Reinisch's market stall
context: Consider farmer Reinisch sells potatoes and carrots from eight hectares at a Saturday village market. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Reinisch acts as an entrepreneur at the stall while village buyers act as households.
Because farmland can theoretically be bought elsewhere, Reinisch's eight hectares should not be treated as scarce.
Potatoes and carrots are goods rather than services even though they must be cooked before eating.
Splitting eight hectares between crops is an economic decision Reinisch cannot avoid given limited land.
Paying cash at the stall is not genuine exchange because only barter counts as real economic trade.
tactical_explanations:
Reinisch produces and sells at the stall, so he acts as an entrepreneur. Village buyers purchasing vegetables act as households.

So the statement is True.

Land somewhere else does not enlarge the eight hectares he actually farms. For his planting decisions that acreage remains fixed and scarce.

So the statement is False.

Potatoes and carrots are tangible produce. Needing to cook them before eating does not turn them into services.

So the statement is True.

Eight hectares cannot grow every crop at once. Splitting the land between uses is an allocation choice he cannot avoid under scarcity.

So the statement is True.

Cash paid for potatoes is money given for goods. Monetary payment is a standard form of exchange, not a non-trade.

So the statement is False.

title: Market day in Hallstatt
context: Consider toni sells cheese wheels; Rosa offers children's face-painting; families buy for groceries or fun. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Toni and Rosa act as entrepreneurs while visiting families act as households.
A cheese wheel is a good and face-painting is a service.
Buying cheese for weekly groceries satisfies a need, while face-painting satisfies more of a want.
Paying for cheese or face-painting fulfils needs or wants through exchange on both sides.
Because Toni has only thirty wheels left, he must economise by allocating stock among queuing families.
tactical_explanations:
Toni and Rosa supply cheese and face-painting as stallholders, so they act as entrepreneurs. Visiting families buy as households.

So the statement is True.

A cheese wheel is a tangible product. Face-painting is an activity performed on the child. Good and service again line up that way.

So the statement is True.

Weekly groceries support basic nutrition, so cheese for the household table meets a need. Face-painting for fun is optional enjoyment, so it meets a want.

So the statement is True.

Money changes hands for cheese or for painting. Each side of the trade gets something it values, which is exchange fulfilling needs or wants.

So the statement is True.

Thirty wheels left is a fixed stock. Toni must decide how to allocate that scarce remaining supply among the queue.

So the statement is True.

title: Scarcity across actors
context: Assess whether scarcity and economising apply uniformly. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A multinational corporation with large cash reserves still faces scarce managerial attention and factory capacity.
Households never economise because their wants are unlimited and budgets therefore do not constrain them.
Governments are excluded from scarcity because they can always raise taxes to fund any project immediately.
Economising is rational behaviour when a resource is limited relative to competing uses.
Entrepreneurs must economise on inputs such as labour hours and raw materials to stay viable.
tactical_explanations:
Cash on the balance sheet does not multiply managerial hours or factory floors. Attention and capacity remain limited among competing projects, so scarcity still binds a large firm.

So the statement is True.

Household wants may be open-ended, but budgets are not. Finite income forces trade-offs, which is exactly economising.

So the statement is False.

Tax capacity and political capital are limited within any budget period. Governments still allocate among projects rather than funding every idea at once.

So the statement is False.

When a resource has more valuable uses than units available, careful prioritisation is the rational response. That is what economising means.

So the statement is True.

Labour hours and raw materials are limited inputs. Entrepreneurs who ignore that limit struggle to stay viable, so economising on inputs is required.

So the statement is True.

title: Elif: tutoring or unpaid internship
context: Consider elif can keep tutoring for 400 euros monthly or take an overlapping unpaid architecture internship. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Accepting the internship means opportunity cost is 400 euros monthly tutoring income forgone.
Because the internship pays nothing, choosing it has no opportunity cost at all.
Keeping tutoring means giving up career experience and prospects from the internship.
Opportunity cost must always be expressed only in euros with no other dimensions allowed.
Elif still allocates scarce time between tutoring and internship despite being a student.
tactical_explanations:
Opportunity cost is the benefit of the next-best alternative she gives up. If Elif takes the internship, she cannot keep the overlapping tutoring, so she forgoes that 400-euro monthly income. That forgone pay is exactly the financial opportunity cost named in the claim.

So the statement is True.

Pay on the chosen path is not what defines opportunity cost. The internship pays zero, yet Elif still gives up the tutoring income she could have earned instead. Zero pay on the internship does not erase that forgone benefit.

So the statement is False.

If she stays with tutoring, the next-best path she turns down is the internship. She therefore forgoes the career experience and architecture prospects that internship would have offered. Those forgone benefits are her opportunity cost of keeping the tutoring.

So the statement is True.

Opportunity cost is the value of the alternative forgone, and that value need not be stated only in euros. Experience, skills, and other non-money dimensions can count. The absolute rule that only euros are allowed is too narrow.

So the statement is False.

Her calendar hours are limited. Tutoring and the internship overlap, so she cannot fully do both. Being a student does not remove that scarcity of time; she still has to allocate the hours between the two uses.

So the statement is True.

title: Simon: car wash or volunteering
context: Consider simon can earn 45 euros at a car wash or volunteer at an animal shelter on the same Saturday. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: If Simon volunteers, the opportunity cost is the 45 euros forgone from the car wash shift.
Scarcity concerns only money, so Simon faces no real scarcity when choosing how to use his Saturday.
Personal satisfaction from volunteering cancels any opportunity cost that might otherwise exist.
Because Simon is a teenager, scarce-resource allocation concepts do not apply to his Saturday.
The shelter's dog food cost is part of Simon's opportunity cost when he chooses volunteering.
tactical_explanations:
Same Saturday, two uses. If Simon volunteers, he cannot take the car wash shift, so he forgoes the 45 euros that shift would have paid. That forgone wage is the financial benefit of his next-best alternative.

So the statement is True.

Scarcity is not limited to money. Saturday hours are finite, and Simon can use them for the car wash or for volunteering, not both fully. Time remains scarce even when cash is not the only concern.

So the statement is False.

Enjoying volunteering may make the choice feel worthwhile, but it does not wipe out what he gives up. He still forgoes the 45-euro car wash wage. Satisfaction and opportunity cost can coexist.

So the statement is False.

Age does not exempt anyone from scarce-resource choices. A teenager still has only one Saturday to allocate between paid work and volunteering, so the usual opportunity-cost logic applies.

So the statement is False.

Opportunity cost is what Simon himself gives up by volunteering, namely the car wash earnings and whatever else he personally forgoes. The shelter's dog food bill is the organisation's cost, not Simon's forgone alternative.

So the statement is False.

title: Three actors, one week
context: Consider the Webers choose holiday versus loan repayment; a firm chooses hire versus vans; a ministry chooses motorway versus railway. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Households, firms, and governments all allocate fixed budgets among competing uses this year.
The holiday's opportunity cost is the benefit of early loan repayment the Webers give up.
Hiring a sales rep means giving up the benefit of upgrading delivery vans instead.
Resurfacing the motorway means giving up the railway extension's benefit for residents.
A teenager's Saturday hours spent studying forfeit paid work income as opportunity cost.
tactical_explanations:
The Webers, the firm, and the ministry each work with a limited budget for the year. Holiday versus repayment, hire versus vans, and motorway versus railway are competing uses of those funds. All three actor types face the same kind of allocation problem.

So the statement is True.

If the Webers take the holiday, they do not use that money for early loan repayment. The benefit of that repayment is the next-best alternative they forgo, so it is the holiday's opportunity cost.

So the statement is True.

The firm can fund either the sales hire or the van upgrade with the same limited resources. Choosing the hire means giving up the delivery-van benefits. That forgone upgrade is the opportunity cost of the hire.

So the statement is True.

The ministry's budget cannot fully deliver both projects. Choosing the motorway resurfacing means residents forgo the railway extension's benefits. That forgone railway benefit is the opportunity cost.

So the statement is True.

A teenager who studies on Saturday cannot also take a paid shift in those same hours. The forgone wage from that job alternative is the financial opportunity cost of studying.

So the statement is True.

title: Misunderstanding opportunity cost
context: Consider robin claims opportunity cost is the sum of every rejected option's price. Sara chooses a 500-euro washer or 700-euro laptop. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: If Sara buys the laptop, opportunity cost is the washer's benefit forgone, not all rejected purchases combined.
Robin's sum-of-all-rejected definition matches the standard economic definition exactly.
Choosing between only two items involves no scarcity because scarcity requires many options.
If Sara buys the washer, opportunity cost is 1,200 euros, the combined price of both items.
Opportunity cost refers to the alternative forgone, not the price of the item actually purchased.
tactical_explanations:
Sara faces two concrete options: the washer and the laptop. Buying the laptop means she forgoes the washer's benefit, which is her next-best alternative. Opportunity cost is that one forgone path, not a pile of every purchase she might ever have rejected.

So the statement is True.

The standard definition uses only the next-best alternative, not the sum of every rejected option's price. Robin's additive rule therefore does not match the economic definition.

So the statement is False.

Scarcity appears whenever limited means meet competing uses. Two options and a limited budget are enough. Sara cannot buy both the washer and the laptop with the same money, so scarcity is present.

So the statement is False.

If she buys the washer, she forgoes the laptop. The relevant figure is the benefit of that 700-euro laptop alternative, not 500 + 700 = 1,200. Adding both prices double-counts and invents a cost she never pays.

So the statement is False.

Opportunity cost asks what she gives up by choosing one path. It is the alternative forgone, not the sticker price of the item she actually buys.

So the statement is True.

title: Bergmann renovation savings
context: Consider the Bergmanns saved 18,000 euros for a full kitchen or full bathroom renovation, affordable only one this year. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: 18,000 euros is a limited resource allocated between kitchen and bathroom projects.
Kitchen renovation means opportunity cost is the bathroom renovation's benefit forgone.
Bathroom renovation means opportunity cost is greater resale value forgone from the kitchen.
Identical 18,000-euro costs mean neither option can have opportunity cost.
As a household, the Bergmanns face the same allocation problem as firms and governments.
tactical_explanations:
They have 18,000 euros saved and can fund only one full renovation this year. That fixed sum is a limited resource that must be allocated to either the kitchen or the bathroom, not both.

So the statement is True.

Choosing the kitchen uses up the savings, so the bathroom renovation does not happen. The bathroom's benefits are the next-best alternative forgone, which is the opportunity cost of the kitchen.

So the statement is True.

Choosing the bathroom means they forgo the kitchen. If the kitchen would have added more to resale value, that greater resale benefit is what they give up. That forgone kitchen payoff is the opportunity cost of the bathroom.

So the statement is True.

Equal price tags do not cancel opportunity cost. Even when both projects cost 18,000 euros, choosing one still means giving up the other project's benefits. Matching costs are not the same as zero forgone benefit.

So the statement is False.

Households, like firms and governments, work with limited resources and competing uses. The Bergmanns' renovation choice is the same basic allocation problem in household clothing.

So the statement is True.

title: Mila: bookstore or swimming academy
context: Consider Mila can earn 60 euros at a bookstore or attend a free academy that might help a sports scholarship. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Saturday morning hours are scarce between the bookstore job and the academy.
Choosing the academy means opportunity cost is 60 euros bookstore earnings forgone.
Choosing the job means opportunity cost is training time and potential scholarship benefit forgone.
Uncertain scholarship benefit cannot count as any kind of opportunity cost.
Individuals face scarce-resource allocation, not only firms and governments.
tactical_explanations:
Saturday morning is one block of hours. Mila can work at the bookstore or attend the academy, but she cannot fully do both at once. Those hours are scarce between the two uses.

So the statement is True.

If she goes to the academy, she skips the bookstore shift and forgoes the 60 euros it would have paid. That forgone wage is the financial opportunity cost of attending.

So the statement is True.

If she takes the job, she misses the academy session. She forgoes the training time and whatever scholarship prospects that session might support. Those forgone benefits are the opportunity cost of working.

So the statement is True.

Uncertainty does not ban a benefit from opportunity-cost thinking. A possible scholarship gain is still a forgone alternative when she works instead. Risk or doubt may change how she weighs it, but it can still count.

So the statement is False.

Individuals allocate scarce time and money just as firms and governments do. Mila's Saturday choice is a personal version of the same scarce-resource problem.

So the statement is True.

title: City hall transport budget
context: Consider city hall has 500,000 euros for a new bus line or protected bike lanes, insufficient for both fully this year. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The government must allocate its limited 500,000-euro budget between two transport projects.
Public projects funded by tax face no opportunity cost because they are not market-priced.
Because both projects improve transport, they cannot be compared using opportunity cost at all.
Choosing bike lanes means opportunity cost is the bus line's benefit for commuters forgone.
Governments are exempt from the basic scarce-resources problem that households and firms face.
tactical_explanations:
City hall has 500,000 euros and cannot fully fund both the bus line and the bike lanes this year. That fixed envelope must be allocated between the two transport projects.

So the statement is True.

Tax finance does not erase trade-offs. Spending the money on one project still means forgoing the other project's benefits. Public funding and the absence of a market price do not cancel opportunity cost.

So the statement is False.

Both projects may improve transport, yet they compete for the same limited budget. Opportunity cost compares those alternative uses: what one project delivers that the other would have delivered instead.

So the statement is False.

Choosing bike lanes uses the budget, so the bus line is not built. Commuters forgo the bus line's benefits. That forgone bus benefit is the opportunity cost of the bike lanes.

So the statement is True.

Governments work with limited budgets and competing programmes just as households and firms do. There is no exemption from the scarce-resources problem.

So the statement is False.

title: Ana: bakery job or market stall
context: Consider ana earns 1,900 euros monthly at a supermarket bakery or could run a stall earning 2,100 euros without job security. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Opportunity cost equals the sum of every rejected alternative's price added together.
Because the stall pays more, Ana's decision to leave carries zero opportunity cost.
If Ana stays, the opportunity cost is the 2,100 euros she could have earned from the stall.
Choosing between two jobs involves no scarcity because she selects between jobs rather than physical goods.
Paid holidays cannot factor into opportunity cost because only euro amounts count.
tactical_explanations:
Opportunity cost is the benefit of the single next-best alternative forgone, not a sum of every rejected option's price. Adding all rejections together overstates the cost and misstates the definition.

So the statement is False.

A higher expected stall income may make leaving attractive, but leaving still means giving up the bakery job's pay and security. Higher expected gain does not drive opportunity cost to zero.

So the statement is False.

If Ana stays at the bakery, her next-best alternative is the stall. She forgoes the 2,100 euros she could have earned there, so that figure is the financial opportunity cost of staying.

So the statement is True.

Labour time is scarce whether the choice is over goods or over jobs. She cannot work both paths fully at once, so choosing between the bakery and the stall is still a scarce-resource allocation.

So the statement is False.

Opportunity cost is the value of what is forgone, and that value is not restricted to pure euro totals. Job security and paid holidays can matter as part of what she keeps or gives up. The claim that only euro amounts ever count is too narrow.

So the statement is False.

title: Nina: agency or freelance
context: Consider nina earns 2,700 euros at a design agency or could freelance for 3,100 euros with self-managed admin. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Freelancing means opportunity cost is 2,700-euro agency salary forgone.
Higher freelance pay eliminates opportunity cost from Nina's decision entirely.
Staying at the agency means opportunity cost is potential 3,100-euro freelance income forgone.
Admin work should be added directly onto salary to calculate opportunity cost by definition.
Working time is limited, so Nina's choice reflects scarce-resource allocation.
tactical_explanations:
If Nina freelances, she gives up the agency job. The next-best alternative's financial benefit is the 2,700-euro salary she forgoes. That forgone salary is the opportunity cost named here.

So the statement is True.

Higher freelance pay may tip her decision, but it does not erase what she gives up. She still forgoes the agency salary and whatever else employment provided. Opportunity cost remains.

So the statement is False.

If she stays at the agency, she forgoes freelancing. The potential 3,100-euro freelance income is the financial benefit of that next-best alternative, so it is the opportunity cost of staying.

So the statement is True.

By definition, opportunity cost is the benefit of the alternative forgone, not a mechanical sum of salary plus hours of admin. Admin burden may affect how she values freelancing, but it is not added onto salary as the definition of opportunity cost.

So the statement is False.

She has limited working time and cannot pursue both career paths fully at once. Choosing agency or freelance is therefore an allocation of a scarce resource.

So the statement is True.

title: Almeida garden plot
context: Consider the Almeidas have forty square metres for vegetables saving 250 euros yearly or flowers they enjoy with no savings. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Forty square metres is a limited resource allocated between vegetables and flowers.
Choosing flowers means opportunity cost is roughly 250 euros annual grocery savings forgone.
Choosing vegetables means giving up enjoyment of a flower garden even if that benefit is non-financial.
Allocating overtime hours to maintenance forgoes backlog revenue that those hours could have earned.
The household faces the same allocation problem as firms and governments with scarce resources.
tactical_explanations:
Forty square metres is a fixed plot. Using it for vegetables means less space for flowers, and the reverse. That land is a limited resource allocated between the two uses.

So the statement is True.

Vegetables would save about 250 euros a year on groceries. Choosing flowers instead forgoes those savings. Roughly 250 euros of annual grocery benefit is therefore the financial opportunity cost of the flower garden.

So the statement is True.

Choosing vegetables means the flower garden does not happen. Enjoyment of flowers is a real benefit even when it is not priced in euros, and forgoing that enjoyment is part of the opportunity cost of growing vegetables.

So the statement is True.

Overtime hours spent on maintenance cannot also clear backlog. The revenue those hours could have earned from backlog work is forgone, so that forgone revenue is the opportunity cost of maintenance.

So the statement is True.

Households, firms, and governments all allocate scarce means among competing uses. The Almeidas' garden choice is the household version of that shared problem.

So the statement is True.

title: Mateo: salary versus freelancing
context: Consider mateo earns 3,600 euros monthly salaried or could freelance for 4,200 euros without employer health insurance. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Mateo allocates limited working time between two competing income paths.
Taking freelance means giving up 3,600-euro salary and employer-paid benefits as opportunity cost.
Staying salaried means giving up potential 4,200-euro freelance income as opportunity cost.
Because he cannot do both full-time, working hours are a scarce resource forcing one choice.
Opportunity cost as the next-best alternative's benefit applies directly to Mateo's decision.
tactical_explanations:
Mateo has one stock of working time and two income paths: salaried employment and freelancing. He must allocate that limited time between those competing uses rather than fully living both.

So the statement is True.

Freelancing means leaving the salaried job. He forgoes the 3,600-euro salary and the employer-paid benefits, including health insurance. Those forgone employment benefits are the opportunity cost of freelancing.

So the statement is True.

Staying salaried means he does not take the freelance path. He forgoes the potential 4,200-euro freelance income, which is the financial benefit of the next-best alternative.

So the statement is True.

He cannot work both full-time careers at once. Working hours are therefore scarce, and that scarcity forces a choice between the two paths.

So the statement is True.

Opportunity cost is defined as the benefit of the next-best alternative given up. Mateo's salary-versus-freelance choice is a direct application of that definition in either direction.

So the statement is True.

title: Retail chain store location
context: Consider a chain can open one store: location A projects 220,000-euro profit, location B 180,000-euro profit. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Available capital this year is scarce and allocated between location A and B.
Opening at A means opportunity cost is 180,000-euro profit from B forgone.
Opening at B means opportunity cost is 400,000 euros, combined profit of both locations.
Large firms' expansion decisions never involve scarce resources because of their size.
This illustrates firms allocating limited resources among competing uses like households do.
tactical_explanations:
The chain can open only one store this year with the capital available. That limited capital must be allocated to either location A or location B, so it is scarce between the two sites.

So the statement is True.

Opening at A means location B is not opened. The next-best alternative's profit is B's projected 180,000 euros, which is therefore the opportunity cost of choosing A.

So the statement is True.

Opportunity cost of opening at B is the profit forgone from A, which is 220,000 euros, not 220,000 + 180,000 = 400,000. Combining both profits invents a total the firm never earns from a single store.

So the statement is False.

Firm size does not create unlimited capital each period. Even a large chain has a finite expansion budget and must choose among sites, so scarce resources still matter.

So the statement is False.

The location choice is a firm allocating limited capital among competing uses, the same basic problem households face with limited budgets.

So the statement is True.

title: Irrigation water: wheat or vegetables
context: Consider farmer Ilić can fully irrigate wheat (12,000-euro revenue) or vegetables (15,500-euro revenue) this month, not both. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Limited irrigation water is scarce and must be allocated between the two field types.
Irrigating vegetables means opportunity cost is 27,500 euros, the combined revenue of both fields.
Because Ilić is a farmer not a registered firm, his decisions involve no opportunity cost.
Irrigating wheat means opportunity cost is 15,500 euros vegetable revenue forgone.
Same-farm fields mean watering one does not count as allocating a scarce resource.
tactical_explanations:
This month's irrigation water is limited and can fully support either wheat or vegetables, not both. That water is scarce and must be allocated between the two field types.

So the statement is True.

Irrigating vegetables forgoes wheat revenue of 12,000 euros, not 12,000 + 15,500 = 27,500. Opportunity cost is the next-best field's revenue, not the sum of both.

So the statement is False.

Legal form does not decide whether opportunity cost exists. A farmer allocating scarce water still forgoes one crop's revenue when watering the other. Registration as a firm is irrelevant.

So the statement is False.

Irrigating wheat means vegetables are not fully irrigated. Vegetable revenue of 15,500 euros is forgone, so that figure is the opportunity cost of watering wheat.

So the statement is True.

Being on the same farm does not make water unlimited. One scarce water supply still forces a choice between wheat and vegetables, which is precisely an allocation problem.

So the statement is False.

title: Factory overtime hours
context: Consider a plant manager can assign limited overtime either to catch up order backlog or to preventive maintenance on Line 2. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Overtime hours are scarce and allocated between backlog clearance and maintenance.
Backlog overtime means opportunity cost is reduced breakdown risk benefit from maintenance forgone.
Maintenance overtime means opportunity cost is delayed-shipment revenue from backlog work forgone.
Overtime is unlimited if workers agree, so no allocation problem exists.
Opportunity cost helps compare competing uses of the same limited hour pool.
tactical_explanations:
The plant has a limited pool of overtime hours. Assigning them to backlog clearance means they are not available for Line 2 maintenance, and the reverse. Those hours are scarce between the two tasks.

So the statement is True.

If overtime clears backlog, preventive maintenance is postponed. The benefit of lower breakdown risk from that maintenance is forgone, and that forgone benefit is the opportunity cost of backlog overtime.

So the statement is True.

If overtime goes to maintenance, backlog work waits. Delayed-shipment revenue that backlog clearance could have protected is forgone, so that forgone revenue is the opportunity cost of maintenance.

So the statement is True.

Worker willingness does not make overtime unlimited. Budgets, fatigue rules, and legal caps still constrain usable hours, so an allocation problem remains.

So the statement is False.

Both uses draw on the same limited overtime pool and deliver different benefits. Opportunity cost is the natural way to compare what one use gains against what the other would have delivered.

So the statement is True.

title: Bergdorf council budget
context: Consider bergdorf has 90,000 euros for either a skate park or a library renovation this year, not both. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Scarcity applies only to money, never to time, land, or labour hours.
Households never face opportunity cost because wants are unlimited and budgets do not constrain them.
Because councils can raise taxes in principle, this year's 90,000-euro budget is not scarce.
Opportunity cost exists only for registered companies, not for individuals or students.
Choosing the library means opportunity cost is the skate park's benefit, not both projects combined.
tactical_explanations:
Money is one scarce resource, not the only one. Time, land, and labour hours are also limited and must be allocated among competing uses. The claim that scarcity never applies to those other resources is wrong.

So the statement is False.

Households have limited budgets even when wants are large. Choosing one purchase means forgoing another, so opportunity cost is a everyday household idea, not something households escape.

So the statement is False.

A future power to raise taxes does not make this year's 90,000-euro envelope unlimited. Within the current year the council can fund either the skate park or the library renovation, not both, so that budget is scarce now.

So the statement is False.

Opportunity cost attaches to any decision-maker who forgoes an alternative, including individuals and students. Company registration is not a prerequisite.

So the statement is False.

Choosing the library means the skate park is not built. Opportunity cost is the skate park's forgone benefit, the next-best alternative, not a combined total of both projects.

So the statement is True.

title: Handwerk GmbH timber choice
context: Consider handwerk GmbH can use its oak batch for dining tables (40,000-euro profit) or bookshelves (28,000-euro profit), not both. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Choosing the lower-return option means opportunity cost is zero because a better option existed.
Personal satisfaction from an activity eliminates any opportunity cost associated with it.
Economising means treating limited resources as if they were unlimited without any prioritisation.
Sharing the same timber means no opportunity cost exists because the wood is used either way.
Limited oak forces economising by selecting the more profitable product line.
tactical_explanations:
Choosing bookshelves (28,000) instead of tables (40,000) still has an opportunity cost: the higher table profit forgone. The existence of a better option is precisely why that cost is large, not why it is zero.

So the statement is False.

Enjoying an activity may make it feel worthwhile, but it does not erase the benefits of the path not taken. Opportunity cost remains the forgone alternative's benefit.

So the statement is False.

Economising means using scarce resources carefully and setting priorities. Treating limited resources as unlimited is the opposite of economising.

So the statement is False.

The oak batch can become tables or bookshelves, not both. Using the wood one way forgoes the other product's profit. Shared limited timber is exactly why opportunity cost arises, not why it disappears.

So the statement is False.

With one oak batch and two product lines, Handwerk must choose. Economising with that scarce timber points toward the more profitable tables (40,000) over bookshelves (28,000).

So the statement is True.

title: Fatima's electric hatchback choice
context: Consider fatima compares buying an electric hatchback with a government bonus versus keeping her petrol car two more years. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Any price change anywhere is automatically macroeconomics regardless of scope analysed.
Because a national bonus programme exists, her purchase automatically becomes macroeconomics instead of micro.
A single café changing cake prices is automatically a macroeconomic event.
Nationwide statistics on total car sales after the bonus would be macroeconomic analysis.
Microeconomics and macroeconomics study identical questions with no meaningful scope difference.
tactical_explanations:
A price change becomes micro or macro only through the unit of analysis. One shop's sticker price, studied on its own, is a micro pricing decision. Macroeconomics looks at general price levels and economy-wide inflation, not every local price move. The absolute claim that any price change is automatically macro fails for that reason.

So the statement is False.

Fatima is still one household weighing two cars under a limited budget. A national bonus may change her net price, but the object of study remains her individual purchase. Policy origin does not flip the scope; an individual choice stays micro unless the analysis shifts to nationwide aggregates.

So the statement is False.

One café resetting cake prices is a single-firm price decision in one product market. That is classic micro territory. Calling it macroeconomic simply because a price moved confuses topic wording with the level of aggregation.

So the statement is False.

Total car sales for the whole country after the bonus summarise an economy-wide outcome. Aggregated national sales and related growth effects belong to macroeconomic analysis.

So the statement is True.

Both branches ask about scarce resources and choices, but they do not ask the same questions at the same scale. Micro zooms in on households, firms, and individual markets; macro zooms out to the whole economy. Treating the scopes as identical erases that distinction.

So the statement is False.

title: Recession headline
context: Consider headlines report two consecutive quarters of falling national GDP and rising job losses economy-wide. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Falling national GDP and economy-wide job losses are macroeconomic phenomena.
One closed shop laying off two staff is macroeconomics because layoffs appear in the headline.
Macroeconomics aims to explain and predict recessions and recovery patterns.
Economics as a whole studies decisions under limited resources at micro and macro levels.
Microeconomics cannot study unemployment because unemployment exists only at macro level.
tactical_explanations:
National GDP and economy-wide job losses are aggregates that describe the whole economy. When those totals fall together across quarters, the phenomena sit squarely in macroeconomics.

So the statement is True.

Two staff leaving one closed shop, studied as that shop's decision, is a micro labour adjustment. Sharing a headline with national job losses does not turn two layoffs into an economy-wide aggregate. Scope of analysis still decides the branch.

So the statement is False.

Recessions and recoveries are whole-economy patterns. Building theories that explain why output and employment swing, and that predict how they may turn, is a central macroeconomic task.

So the statement is True.

Economics is the study of decisions under limited resources. Micro and macro share that foundation; they simply apply it at different scales, from individual units up to the entire economy.

So the statement is True.

Unemployment appears in national statistics, but firms still hire and fire, and households still weigh job risk. Microeconomics can study those unit-level labour decisions. The claim that unemployment exists only as a macro topic is too absolute.

So the statement is False.

title: Freonia quarterly report
context: Consider freonia's statistics office reports national growth, unemployment, and central-bank interest rates each quarter. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: This whole-economy report is macroeconomic analysis rather than a single unit's decision.
Growth, unemployment, and interest rates are macroeconomic topics alongside inflation and price levels.
One bakery studying only its own sales and staffing would be microeconomics.
Economics as a science builds theories to explain and predict such nationwide phenomena.
Both branches fall under economics defined as decisions under limited resources.
tactical_explanations:
The Freonia report tracks national growth, unemployment, and policy rates for the country as a whole. That is analysis of economy-wide indicators, not one household's or firm's private decision, so it is macroeconomic.

So the statement is True.

Growth, unemployment, and interest rates sit with inflation and general price levels among the standard whole-economy variables. The report is listing classic macroeconomic topics.

So the statement is True.

A bakery that looks only at its own sales and staffing is studying one firm. That unit-level operational analysis is microeconomics.

So the statement is True.

Economics builds theories so that observed behaviour can be explained and future effects predicted. Nationwide growth and unemployment are exactly the sort of aggregate outcomes that scientific economic theory targets.

So the statement is True.

Micro and macro are branches of one discipline. Both rest on the idea that limited resources force choices, whether the chooser is a single unit or the economy taken as a whole.

So the statement is True.

title: Household heating bill
context: Consider the Weiss family compares gas versus heat-pump suppliers for next winter's contract, ignoring national energy policy. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Macroeconomics cannot explain recessions because only micro markets exist.
Energy is always macroeconomics because heating affects national consumption statistics.
If policymakers analysed total household energy use affecting national inflation, that would be macroeconomics.
Economics studies such household trade-offs under a limited monthly budget.
Micro and macro ask identical questions, so analysing the Weiss family equals analysing the nation.
tactical_explanations:
Macroeconomics exists precisely to explain economy-wide downturns, output gaps, and related aggregates. Individual markets do not exhaust the subject; recession theory is a macro task. The claim that macro cannot explain recessions is wrong.

So the statement is False.

Energy can be studied as one family's heating contract or as national consumption and inflation. Topic labels alone do not decide the branch; the level of analysis does. Calling every energy question macro overreaches.

So the statement is False.

Once the object of study is total household energy use and its effect on national inflation, the analysis has moved to economy-wide aggregates. That is macroeconomic scope.

So the statement is True.

The Weiss family is choosing under a limited monthly budget between competing heating options. Household trade-offs of that kind are core economic subject matter, especially at the micro level.

So the statement is True.

Studying one family's contract is not the same question as studying the whole economy. Micro and macro share a scarcity foundation, but their scopes differ, so the Weiss family analysis does not equal a national analysis.

So the statement is False.

title: Export statistics release
context: Consider the trade ministry publishes total national exports and imports for the year. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Whole-country export and import totals are macroeconomic statistics.
One exporting winery's shipment schedule to Germany is macroeconomics because trade crosses a border.
Macro topics include growth, unemployment, inflation, and interest rates alongside aggregates like trade totals.
Economics tries to explain why national export performance changes over time.
Microeconomics studies individual firms' export decisions when those firms are the unit analysed.
tactical_explanations:
Country-wide export and import totals summarise trade for the economy as a whole. Those aggregates are macroeconomic statistics.

So the statement is True.

One winery's shipment schedule, examined on its own, is a firm-level logistics and pricing decision. Crossing a border does not automatically make the analysis macro; the unit studied is still a single business.

So the statement is False.

Macroeconomics covers growth, unemployment, inflation, and interest rates, and it also works with other aggregates such as national trade totals. The list of topics fits that branch.

So the statement is True.

Explaining why a country's export performance rises or falls over time is an aggregate question. Economics builds theories for exactly that kind of nationwide pattern.

So the statement is True.

When the unit of analysis is one firm choosing whether and how to export, the study is microeconomic. Firm-level export decisions belong in micro whenever that is the scope.

So the statement is True.

title: Confusing scope with topic
context: Consider students debate whether 'prices' and 'jobs' are always macro or micro topics. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Micro and macro study identical questions with no meaningful difference in scope.
Any discussion of wages is automatically macroeconomics because labour markets are national.
Economy-wide average wage growth published by a statistics office is macroeconomics.
A household choosing between two job offers compares micro-level alternatives under limited time.
Economics cannot explain individual choices, only nationwide aggregates.
tactical_explanations:
The meaningful difference is scope. Micro asks about individual households, firms, and markets; macro asks about economy-wide aggregates. Saying the questions are identical erases that split.

So the statement is False.

Wages can be a firm's pay scale or a national average. Labour markets have national dimensions, but that does not force every wage discussion into macro. Classification follows the unit analysed, not the word "wages" alone.

So the statement is False.

An economy-wide average wage growth figure from a statistics office is an aggregate for the whole labour market. That is macroeconomic.

So the statement is True.

Choosing between two job offers allocates scarce time and effort for one household. That comparison of alternatives is micro-level labour allocation.

So the statement is True.

Economics explains and predicts both individual choices and nationwide aggregates. Limiting the subject to aggregates only would discard microeconomics entirely.

So the statement is False.

title: Teacher's scope quiz
context: Consider a teacher lists examples and asks which are micro versus macro. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Micro examines individual households, businesses, or markets; macro examines the whole economy.
A single consumer choosing organic milk is microeconomics.
National unemployment rate is macroeconomics.
Economics explains and predicts at both scopes using theories about limited resources.
If an example mentions government, it must always be classified as macroeconomics.
tactical_explanations:
The usual textbook split is exactly this: micro looks at individual households, businesses, or markets, while macro looks at the economy as a whole. That is the core scope distinction.

So the statement is True.

One consumer picking organic milk is a single household's product choice. That is microeconomics.

So the statement is True.

The national unemployment rate summarises joblessness across the entire economy. That indicator is macroeconomic.

So the statement is True.

Both branches use theories about limited resources to explain what happened and to predict what may happen next. Explanation and prediction are not reserved for one scope only.

So the statement is True.

Government can appear in a local permit for one project or in a nationwide policy that moves aggregates. Mentioning government does not force a macro label; the analysed scope still decides.

So the statement is False.

title: BrewPeak espresso price hike
context: Consider inês raises BrewPeak espresso prices after imported bean costs rise, thinking only about her Porto shop. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: National unemployment figures belong to microeconomics because each worker is an individual.
Macroeconomics is simply the study of any price change, including one café's espresso price.
Microeconomics never studies how two firms interact in one product market.
Macroeconomics refuses to discuss inflation because inflation starts in single shops.
Economics remains a science building theories to explain and predict behaviour despite imperfect human prediction.
tactical_explanations:
National unemployment figures are aggregates for the whole labour market. The fact that each worker is a person does not pull those totals into microeconomics; the published rate is a macro indicator.

So the statement is False.

Inês changing BrewPeak's espresso price for her Porto shop is one firm's pricing response. Macroeconomics studies general price levels and inflation, not every individual café menu change. Equating macro with any price move is wrong.

So the statement is False.

Microeconomics routinely studies how firms interact in a product market, including rivalry, pricing responses, and market structure. The claim that micro never studies two-firm interaction is false.

So the statement is False.

Inflation is a central macroeconomic topic: the general price level across the economy. Even if price rises begin in individual shops, macro still analyses the aggregate movement. It does not refuse the subject.

So the statement is False.

Economics remains a science because it builds theories that explain and predict behaviour, even though foresight is imperfect. That scientific aim holds for Inês's pricing choice and for larger aggregates alike.

So the statement is True.

title: Micro scope traps
context: Analyze traps students face when classifying examples as microeconomic rather than macroeconomic. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A single farmer choosing between wheat and vegetable crops on limited irrigation water is microeconomics.
A single bakery setting its loaf price after flour costs rise is microeconomics.
A city bus company setting a new single-route fare is microeconomics when only that firm's pricing is analysed.
National GDP growth rate publication is macroeconomics because it summarises the entire economy.
Microeconomics can explain and predict behaviour of individual markets, households, and firms.
tactical_explanations:
One farmer allocating limited irrigation water between crops is a single producer's resource choice. That unit-level allocation is microeconomics.

So the statement is True.

One bakery resetting its loaf price after flour costs rise is a firm-level pricing decision studied alone. That is microeconomic analysis.

So the statement is True.

When only the bus company's own route fare is analysed, the scope stays with one firm. Single-firm fare setting under that lens is microeconomics.

So the statement is True.

Published national GDP growth summarises output for the entire economy. That whole-economy indicator is macroeconomic.

So the statement is True.

Microeconomics builds theories precisely to explain and predict how individual markets, households, and firms behave. That is its scientific role at unit scope.

So the statement is True.

title: Ride-hail surge pricing
context: Consider one ride-hail platform raises fares in one city district after a concert ends. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Studying surge pricing for one platform in one district is microeconomics.
Surge pricing is macroeconomics because many riders are affected at once.
If analysts measured whether district fare spikes raised the city's overall consumer price index, that index move would be macroeconomics.
Economics can predict how riders and drivers respond to a local price spike.
Individual market pricing never falls within economics because only governments set prices.
tactical_explanations:
One platform's surge pricing in one district is a single-market pricing episode. Studying that platform's local fare response is microeconomics.

So the statement is True.

Many riders can be affected without turning the analysis into macro. Macro requires economy-wide aggregates, not merely a crowded local market. Participant count alone does not reclassify the scope.

So the statement is False.

A city's overall consumer price index is a general price-level measure. If analysts ask whether local fare spikes moved that index, they have shifted to aggregate price measurement, which is macroeconomic.

So the statement is True.

Economics builds theories of how buyers and sellers respond to prices. Predicting rider and driver reactions to a local spike applies that microeconomic toolkit.

So the statement is True.

Firms set market prices all the time; that is central microeconomic subject matter. The claim that only governments set prices, and that market pricing falls outside economics, is false.

So the statement is False.

title: Competition authority case
context: Consider regulators investigate whether three mobile carriers colluded on text-message pricing nationally. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Investigating pricing across an entire national mobile market can involve macro-style market-wide analysis.
One subscriber choosing a cheaper text plan for her own phone is microeconomics.
Economics builds theories to explain firm behaviour and market outcomes including competition issues.
Microeconomics studies individual firm pricing strategies when one carrier alone is analysed.
Economics excludes market competition because only government budgets matter.
tactical_explanations:
A probe of pricing across the entire national mobile market looks at market-wide structure and outcomes, not one subscriber's bill. That market-wide lens can involve macro-style analysis of the whole market.

So the statement is True.

A single subscriber picking a cheaper text plan is ordinarily a household decision. In this case, though, the investigation concerns national carrier pricing across the mobile market, and the claim treats the subscriber side-choice as if it settles that market-wide classification. Keeping the regulator probe separate from one phone plan means the sentence does not hold as framed here.

So the statement is False.

Economics builds theories to explain how firms behave and how markets turn out, including competition and collusion questions. Those explanatory targets sit inside the subject.

So the statement is True.

When only one carrier's pricing strategy is analysed, the unit is a single firm. That firm-level pricing study is microeconomics.

So the statement is True.

Market competition is core microeconomic and industrial-organisation subject matter. Economics does not exclude it in favour of government budgets alone.

So the statement is False.

title: Bookstore pricing experiment
context: Consider a regional bookstore chain tests a 5% price cut in one city branch and tracks only that branch's weekly revenue. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Analysing one branch's revenue after its own price change is microeconomics.
Central bank inflation targeting for an entire currency area is macroeconomics.
If the national statistics office later reported economy-wide consumer price inflation, that would be macroeconomics.
Micro focuses on individual households, businesses, and markets rather than the whole economy.
Economics tries to explain and predict outcomes such as how a branch responds to a price cut.
tactical_explanations:
Tracking one branch's weekly revenue after its own price cut keeps the analysis on a single business unit. That revenue response is microeconomic.

So the statement is True.

Inflation targeting for an entire currency area is a whole-economy price-stability policy. That policy scope is macroeconomic.

So the statement is True.

Economy-wide consumer price inflation reported by the national statistics office is a general price-level aggregate. Reporting that figure is macroeconomic.

So the statement is True.

Microeconomics focuses on individual households, businesses, and markets rather than on the economy taken as a whole. That is the standard scope split.

So the statement is True.

Economics aims to explain and predict outcomes such as how one branch's sales respond to a price cut. Branch-level response prediction is exactly that scientific aim at micro scope.

So the statement is True.

title: Kelvinia rate rise
context: Consider kelvinia's central bank raises the key interest rate nationwide to slow inflation. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: GDP growth and one household's grocery list are analysed with identical tools and the same scope.
Interest rates on national policy are a micro topic because each loan is signed by one borrower.
Microeconomics covers only diagrams; macroeconomics covers only newspaper opinion.
Because mortgages of specific families change, the central-bank move is automatically microeconomics.
Economics tries to build theories explaining why central banks raise rates and predict inflation effects.
tactical_explanations:
GDP growth is an economy-wide aggregate; a grocery list is one household's allocation problem. They are not analysed with the same scope, even if both involve scarce resources.

So the statement is False.

A nationwide policy rate is a macro instrument aimed at inflation for the whole economy. The fact that each mortgage is signed by one borrower does not pull national interest-rate policy into microeconomics.

So the statement is False.

Both branches use theories, data, and models; neither is limited to diagrams or newspaper opinion. Reducing micro to pictures and macro to commentary misstates what economics does.

So the statement is False.

Specific families may refinance after the rate rise, but those individual effects do not reclassify a whole-economy central-bank move as microeconomics. The policy still targets nationwide inflation.

So the statement is False.

Economics builds theories that explain why central banks raise rates and that predict how inflation and spending may respond. That explanatory and predictive aim is part of economics as a science.

So the statement is True.

title: Household savings rate national data
context: Consider central bank publishes average household savings rate across the entire country. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Average national household savings rate is a macroeconomic aggregate.
One family increasing its monthly savings by fifty euros is macroeconomics because saving is national policy topic.
Macro includes growth, unemployment, inflation, interest rates, and such economy-wide averages.
Economics explains and predicts how aggregate saving responds to interest rate changes.
Microeconomics studies one family's saving choice when that family alone is the unit analysed.
tactical_explanations:
An average household savings rate for the entire country is an economy-wide statistic. That aggregate belongs in macroeconomics.

So the statement is True.

One family raising monthly saving by fifty euros, studied on its own, is a household budget choice. Calling it macro merely because saving also appears in national policy debates confuses topic with scope.

So the statement is False.

Macroeconomics covers growth, unemployment, inflation, and interest rates, and it also works with economy-wide averages such as the national savings rate. Those sit together as macro variables.

So the statement is True.

How aggregate saving responds when interest rates change is a whole-economy question. Economics builds theories to explain and predict that aggregate link.

So the statement is True.

When the unit analysed is one family alone, its saving choice is microeconomics. Single-household portfolio and budget decisions stay at that scope.

So the statement is True.

title: Startup funding round
context: Consider ten startups in a city receive venture funding; an analyst studies only one robotics firm's hiring plan. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Choosing a smartphone brand is classified as macroeconomics once the price exceeds €500.
Because venture capital is a national phenomenon, any firm-level study becomes macroeconomics.
Summing all startup investment in the country to assess economic growth would be macroeconomics.
Microeconomics explains and predicts behaviour of individual businesses and markets.
Economics excludes entrepreneurial firms because they are too small for scientific study.
tactical_explanations:
